questions.question: What is medicine, and what are change and continuity in the history of medicine?
questions.expected_answer: Medicine is the knowledge and practice of preventing, diagnosing and treating illness and injury, and also a substance used to treat illness. Change means the ways ideas and practices have changed over time, such as now understanding germs. Continuity means the ways things have stayed the same, such as people still using plants as medicines today.

questions.question: Describe medicine in ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome.
questions.expected_answer: Ancient Egyptian doctors wrote remedies on papyrus, set broken bones and put honey on wounds, but also used prayers and charms. In Greece, Hippocrates taught that illness has natural causes and that doctors should observe patients carefully, though the Greek idea of four humours was wrong. The Romans built aqueducts, public baths and sewers to keep people healthy, and Galen studied anatomy by dissecting animals.

questions.question: How did the Islamic world and the Renaissance change medicine?
questions.expected_answer: Islamic scholars in cities such as Baghdad, Cairo and Córdoba translated Greek medical books, added new knowledge and built hospitals, and Ibn Sina wrote The Canon of Medicine, used in Europe for centuries. In the Renaissance, people questioned old ideas: Vesalius published detailed drawings of the human body in 1543, correcting Galen's mistakes, and Harvey showed in 1628 that the heart pumps blood around the body. The printing press spread these ideas.
